summary: Scan the map; every time we find land we haven't visited yet, it is a new island, so we count it and flood-fill all land connected to it with a BFS (T9 — BFS flood fill, with T8 grid neighbours). The `seen` table makes sure each island is counted once.

blocks.title: Read the map
blocks.text: `R C` on one line, then the program prints `Enter the map:` and reads R rows with no prompt. We keep the rows as strings because we never change them — visited cells are tracked separately.

blocks.title: Visited table and counter
blocks.text: `seen[r][c]` becomes True once a land cell belongs to a counted island. Build it with a comprehension — `[[False] * C] * R` would share one row.

blocks.title: Find land we haven't visited
blocks.text: Check every cell. `'#'` that is not `seen` yet must be the start of a brand-new island.

blocks.title: Count it and start the flood
blocks.text: Add 1 to the island count, mark the cell seen **before** putting it in the queue, and start the BFS from it. Marking when adding (not when removing) stops cells from being queued twice.

blocks.title: Take the next cell
blocks.text: Keep going until the queue is empty — then the whole island is marked.

blocks.title: Spread to connected land
blocks.text: Only up, down, left and right — diagonals do NOT connect. The bounds check comes first so `grid[-1]` never wraps to the last row. Each new land cell is marked and queued.

complexity: Time O(R·C): every cell is visited a constant number of times; with 100×100 that is 10,000 cells.
pitfalls: Adding diagonal directions — they must NOT connect.
Marking cells seen only when popped → the same cell is queued many times.
